Which ancient Greco-Roman treatise formulated this quintessential definition of elevated aesthetic experience?
items.explanation: Pseudo-Longinus wrote 'Peri Hypsous' ('On the Sublime', 1st century AD), identifying grandeur of thought and noble passion as the primary innate sources of the Sublime.

items.title: Game 4 (💬 Who Said It?) · Level 10 · Quote #8
items.meta: Work: On the Sublime (Section 1) · Transport vs Persuasion
items.stem:
“The effect of elevated language upon an audience is not persuasion, but transport (ekstasis)... A well-timed stroke of sublimity scatters everything before it like a thunderbolt.”

Who distinguished sublime transport from rhetorical persuasion?
items.explanation: Longinus observed that while rhetoric aims at rational persuasion, the true Sublime sweeps the listener off their feet with overwhelming emotional ecstasy ('ekstasis').

items.title: Game 4 (💬 Who Said It?) · Level 10 · Quote #9
items.meta: Work: Ars Poetica · Utile Dulci
items.stem:
“Aut prodesse volunt aut delectare poetae” (“Poets aim either to benefit, or to please, or to say what is both enjoyable and helpful to life”).

Which Roman poet formulated the doctrine of combining profit with delight (utile dulci)?
items.explanation: Horace formulated this famous criterion in 'Ars Poetica' (Epistle to the Pisos, c. 19 BC), asserting that he who blends instruction with delight wins every vote.

items.title: Game 4 (💬 Who Said It?) · Level 10 · Quote #10
items.meta: Work: Ars Poetica · Ut Pictura Poesis
items.stem:
“Ut pictura poesis” (“As is painting, so is poetry”).

Which ancient author penned this celebrated phrase establishing the analogy between poetic and visual arts?
items.explanation: Horace wrote line 361 of 'Ars Poetica' comparing poetry to painting—some works look better up close, others from a distance; some bear repeated scrutiny, others please only once.

items.title: Game 4 (💬 Who Said It?) · Level 10 · Quote #11
items.meta: Work: Ars Poetica · In Medias Res
items.stem: Which Roman poet instructed epic writers to plunge their audience straight into the middle of the action (“in medias res”) rather than beginning from the twin egg of Leda (“ab ovo”)?
items.explanation: Horace praised Homer in 'Ars Poetica' for rushing headlong into the action ('in medias res') of the Trojan War instead of plodding through Helen's mythological birth.

items.title: Game 4 (💬 Who Said It?) · Level 10 · Quote #12
items.meta: Work: An Apology for Poetry · The Poet Never Lieth
items.stem:
“Now for the poet, he nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth. For, as I take it, to lie is to tell that which is not true, so as you would have it believed true; but the poet never maketh any circles about your imagination...”

Who defended imaginative poetry against the charge of lying in 1595?
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney answered Plato's and the Puritans' charge that poets are liars in 'An Apology for Poetry' (1595), arguing that fiction makes no claim to literal factual truth and thus cannot deceive.

items.title: Game 4 (💬 Who Said It?) · Level 10 · Quote #13
items.meta: Work: An Apology for Poetry · Superiority Over History and Philosophy
items.stem:
“The final end of all earthly learning being virtuous action, the poet doth peerless surpass both the moral philosopher and the historian.”

Who declared the poet superior to both philosopher and historian because the poet couples general precept with vivid particular example?
items.explanation: Sidney argued that the philosopher teaches only obscure abstractions that fail to move men to action, while the historian is tied to what was rather than what ought to be; only the poet moves the soul toward virtue.

items.title: Game 4 (💬 Who Said It?) · Level 10 · Quote #14
items.meta: Work: An Apology for Poetry · The Golden World
items.stem:
“Nature never set forth the earth in so rich tapestry as divers poets have done... Her world is brazen, the poets only deliver a golden.”

Who wrote this glorious Renaissance defense of imaginative creation?
items.explanation: Sidney celebrated the divine creative spark of the poet ('maker'), who does not merely reproduce fallen fallen brazen nature, but freely creates an idealized 'golden' world.

items.title: Game 4 (💬 Who Said It?) · Level 10 · Quote #15
items.meta: Work: The Schoole of Abuse · Anti-Theatrical Tract
items.stem: Which Puritan pamphleteer dedicated his 1579 anti-theatrical polemic The Schoole of Abuse to Sir Philip Sidney, calling poets 'the fathers of lies' and provoking Sidney's famous Apology?
items.explanation: Stephen Gosson wrote 'The Schoole of Abuse, Conteining a Pleasaunt Invective against Poets, Pipers, Plaiers, Jesters and such like Caterpillers of a Commonwealth' (1579), foolishly dedicating it to Sidney, who was deeply offended and composed his 'Defence/Apology' in rebuttal.
